# research

## Taxonomizing AI Acceptance

People keep announcing where they stand on AI-generated content. This page collects interesting such announcements that I've stumbled across, and files them into a roughly-continuous taxonomy.

The positions taken aren't always exclusively about software-engineering, but that's my industry and I do agree that [Code Goes First](https://sundaylettersfromsam.substack.com/p/code-goes-first) so we see it a lot. Writing, e-mails, images and video all make appearances here, too: this is about the thinking machines writ large.

It files positions, not people. A person can take one position one day, another the next, and that's great, actually! I don't plan to stalk all these sources and keep up to date on what they do, but if I notice a change, I'll move their history to the category I think they're *currently* in. The things each of them has said about each stance they've taken should be far more interesting than the people themselves and where they stand today... this is a phenomenon, not a Pokedex.

The argument that produced this taxonomy - what these positions *are*, where we've seen them before, and what I predict they do next - is in [The Software-Engineering Amish](/2026/10/28/software-engineering-amish.html). This page is the curio shelf, displaying the slice of the world that was interesting to me, as I encountered it.

## The Taxonomy

| Position | Who draws the line | How absolute | The tell |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Amish** | A community, binding its members | Set by the community, with a stated threshold | A vote, a policy, or a house rule you accept by staying |
| **Old Order** | An individual | Near-total, for their own work | They write it by hand, with at most a named exception or two |
| **Mennonite** | An individual | Partial, with a practicable clause | A line at one kind of use, and stated uses on the other side of it |
| **Luddite** | An individual, aimed at everyone | Aimed at changing the world, not just their own practice | Organize, regulate, refuse in public, persuade others to stop |
| **Romantic** | Nobody - the line has already moved past them | Not a rule, a grief | They have accepted the new order and are mourning the old one |
| **English** | Nobody | No line | Full adoption, no stated boundary, enthusiasm - the Amish word for the rest of us |

The names are borrowed on purpose. The real Amish are selective, slow adopters who decide as a community what to allow - Kevin Kelly spoke of [Amish hackers](https://kk.org/thetechnium/amish-hackers-a/) - and the real Luddites had specific asks about wages and the pace of specific machines, not a war on machinery itself. The [Romantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism) here are the nineteenth-century kind, mourning handcraft from inside the industrial England that replaced it. The colloquial versions of these words are the archetypes; the historical ones are more useful.

## Amish

A community draws the line and binds its members to it. The drawn line becomes a defining characteristic of the community as members choose to either abide and stay, or reject and leave.

---

> We are a place for people to collaborate and improve software together. Within this context, the recent votes can be understood as a reconfirmation of those principles: As we want to center on human collaboration, we will not actively support or engage in the creation of LLMs and will not put our limited resources to use for storing single-use software that would pollute our FLOSS commons.
> <br><br>
> -- Bastian Greshake Tzovaras, Otto Richter, and William Zijl (Codeberg), [Protecting our FLOSS commons from LLMs](https://blog.codeberg.org/protecting-our-floss-commons-from-llms.html), July 23, 2026

The members voted 358 to 144 for the rules this quote argues for - majority threshold, member-sourced and deliberate.

---

> It's fine to use LLMs to answer questions, analyze, distill, refine, check, suggest, review. But not to **create.**
> <br>[...]<br>
> We treat PRs as an indication that someone is interested in joining our community and being mentored to work on future PRs.
> <br><br>
> -- Jynn Nelson (for rust-lang/rust), [rust-lang/rust is adopting an LLM policy](https://blog.rust-lang.org/inside-rust/2026/08/05/rust-langrust-is-adopting-an-llm-policy/), August 5, 2026

The line is drawn around review and disclosure, because a polished PR no longer carries that signal on its own. The rule is downstream of the values the community wants to uphold.

---

> The long story short, if your project uses AI, is made by AI, or is intended for AI, it's not welcome on r/opensource. AI, as it exists today, is incongruent to this Open Source community.
> <br><br>
> -- Wolvereness (r/opensource), [Your tokens aren't valuable: No more AI](https://www.reddit.com/r/opensource/comments/1xelcuf/your_tokens_arent_valuable_no_more_ai/), October 24, 2026

A moderator decree, not a member vote - same position as Codeberg, opposite procedure.

## Old Order

An individual draws a near-total line for their own work.

---

> When I code, I don't use AI and I don't even use code completion, this post is about why not. [...] When you code without AI and without code completion you eventually remember much by heart and you become good at looking things up directly in the relevant documentation, and this is really important. [...] Always grabbing the easy way out is never good if what you're doing is important to you or others.
> <br><br>
> -- unixdigest, [The reason why i don't use AI or even code completion](https://unixdigest.com/articles/the-reason-why-i-dont-use-ai-or-even-code-completion.html), May 1, 2025

A near-total personal line extending even to IDE autocomplete, on the analogy of memorizing phone numbers: convenience atrophies the muscle of reading documentation directly and internalizing syntax.

---

> I choose to avoid using "AI" (by which I mean Large Language Models). Here's why: they have a devastating environmental impact, they are trained by exploiting and traumatising millions of low-paid workers, they produce biased and dangerously incorrect results, and they unfairly use people's creative work.
> <br><br>
> -- Andy Balaam, [Why I don't use AI](https://artificialworlds.net/blog/2025/12/16/why-i-dont-use-ai/), December 16, 2025

The ethical case, stated as a list and argued at length.

---

> I have, to date, not used any AI coding tools, at all. I've actively removed them from my IDE. I don't want them. Not just because of questions of their quality (still lower than a human), or because I will miss writing elegant code (I know I will), but because I want my daughter to have a future, and a planet on which to live. Because I actually do care about respecting copyright. But, at this point, it's become obvious that I have to either compromise on that, or leave tech entirely. And every time I think about that, I get angry.
> <br><br>
> -- Larry Garfield, [Selfish AI](https://www.garfieldtech.com/blog/selfish-ai), February 1, 2026

He actively stripped AI tools from his editor out of environmental, copyright, and ethical convictions. His post captures the exact friction of holding an Old Order line as the mainstream defaults shift: the agonizing realization that the collective surrender to "it is what it is" leaves individual holdouts facing a forced choice between ethical compromise and leaving the tech industry entirely.

---

> The thing is that even if I was wrong (I'm not) and AI was somehow helpful for software engineering (it isn't), I still wouldn't want to use it.
> 
> Might I be wrong? I don't know, maybe? Might I be left behind in my industry? I guess, but I don't think it's likely. But honestly I would rather be wrong and left behind than spend my days prompting an AI to do my chosen ***craft***, something I love.
> <br><br>
> -- Anthony Manning-Franklin, [I Will Never Use AI to Code (or write)](https://antman-does-software.com/i-will-never-use-ai-to-code-or-write), March 4, 2026

---

> For example, I've got these color-changing lights. They speak a protocol I've never heard of, and I have no idea where to even begin. I could spend a month digging through manuals and working it out from scratch - or I could ask an LLM to write a client library for me. The security consequences are minimal, it's a constrained use case that I can verify by hand, and I wouldn't be pushing tech debt on anyone else. I still write plenty of code, and I could stop any time. What would be the harm?
>
> Right?
>
> ... Right?
> <br><br>
> -- Kyle Kingsbury, [The Future of Everything is Lies, I Guess: Where Do We Go From Here?](https://aphyr.com/posts/420-the-future-of-everything-is-lies-i-guess-where-do-we-go-from-here), April 16, 2026

He says he's never used an LLM for his writing, software, or personal life, and in the [Work installment](https://aphyr.com/posts/418-the-future-of-everything-is-lies-i-guess-work) two days earlier wrote that he is "not confident I will hold out forever." Still Old Order for now, with the exact shape of a possible move to Mennonite already on the page.

---

> To put it simply: I do not like this world where people are using AI to generate art, music, writing, and software. So I will not use AI.
> <br><br>
> -- Brett, [I'm done using AI](https://brettcodes.com/im-done-using-ai/), August 10, 2026

Twenty years of programming, eighteen months of Claude Code and similar harnesses, then none. His post closes: "Here's to writing code by hand." A migration - English to Old Order - in his own words.

---

> When people claim that it's no longer sustainable to write code by hand, they're not entirely wrong, but only in the same way that it's no longer sustainable to sleep in a bed once someone has taken a shit in it. You want changes? Go ask your agent or something. I'm told that's what you're supposed to do now. I'm out.
> <br><br>
> -- Paul Battley (po-ru), [Why I'm no longer updating this repository](https://po-ru.com/2026/10/18/why-im-no-longer-updating-this-repository), October 18, 2026

He archived his Ruby gems rather than keep contributing to a commons he takes to be strip-mined, after his companion post, "[All our houses are built on sand now](https://po-ru.com/2026/10/07/all-our-houses-are-built-on-sand-now)" (October 7, 2026), found disclosed LLM commits already in the C compilers underneath every language toolchain.

## Mennonites

An individual draws a line with a practicable clause - this far, for these uses, and no farther.

---

> I chose to make using AI a manual action, because I felt the slow loss of competence over time when I relied on it, and I recommend everyone to be cautious with making AI a key part of their workflow.
> <br><br>
> -- Luciano Nooijen, [Why I stopped using AI code editors](https://lucianonooijen.com/blog/why-i-stopped-using-ai-code-editors/), April 1, 2025

He removed AI from his editors and still uses LLMs occasionally, by hand, on purpose. The line is at the editor integration, not at the tool. He tried the English approach and found it not to his taste, settling back at a more deliberate, limited use.

---

> I'm defaulting to pen and paper, I'm defaulting to coding the first draft of that function on my own. [...] I'm writing the plan. I'm the senior dev. The LLM is the assistant.
> <br><br>
> -- Alberto Fortin (via Simon Willison), [After months of coding with LLMs, I'm going back to using my brain](https://simonwillison.net/2025/May/20/after-months-of-coding-with-llms), May 20, 2025

Cut back rather than quit, after LLM-driven rewrites produced a codebase he compared to ten junior developers locked in a room without seeing each other's work.

---

> Now, I would be lying if I said I didn't use LLMs to generate code. I still use Claude, but I do so in a more controlled manner. I copy-paste files that I think are necessary to provide the context, and then I copy-paste code and ask it to make changes to it or write tests for it. This friction has several benefits. [...] It turns code generation from a passive action to a deliberate thoughtful action. It also keeps my brain engaged and active, which means I can still enter the flow state.
> <br><br>
> -- Abhinav Omprakash, [I Am Happier Writing Code by Hand](https://www.abhinavomprakash.com/posts/i-am-happier-writing-code-by-hand/?ref=birchtree.me), February 7, 2026

He deleted Claude Code three times after finding that full-agent vibe coding left him with lethargy and brain fog, rediscovering the joy of coding by hand each time. He now restricts LLMs to manual, deliberate copy-pasting for small diffs and test cases - drawing the line at agentic automation to preserve engagement and flow.

---

> Given the freedom to choose, I’d probably pick a middle path: use LLMs to generate boilerplate code, write tricky test cases, debug nasty issues I can’t think of, and quickly prototype ideas to test. I’m not an AI vegan.
>
> But when it comes to code I write for myself—which includes the code that runs this website—I’m going to continue writing it myself, line by line, like I always did.
> <br><br>
> -- Ankur Sethi, [I'm no longer using coding assistants on personal projects](https://ankursethi.com/blog/coding-assistants-personal-projects/), April 4, 2026

He types every line of his current Django project himself, still uses Claude Code as a search engine and debugger, and follows his clients' rules at work. The line runs between personal and client work.

---

> I use AI tools sparingly for assistance while refactoring code in languages I understand. I occasionally use it to help compose command line arguments for tools like `ffmpeg`. I never use AI to generate images, video, or prose.
> <br><br>
> -- Ky Decker, [Do I belong in tech anymore?](https://ky.fyi/posts/ai-burnout), April 24, 2026

Right after that paragraph, the post notes that AI "feels inescapable," and closes on a five-line creed ("Things that are worth doing are worth doing well... There are no shortcuts"). The creed is absolute; the clause above is why it files here and not one section up.

---

> For programming, I ask it how to do things I don't know how to do. Then I use what I've learned in my own code.
> <br><br>
> -- Derek Sivers, [AI usage](https://sive.rs/ai), updated September 28, 2026

The line sits between asking and generating. The same update adds that he has started using Codex to write unit tests against functions he wrote his way - the "practicable clause," widening in public.

## Luddites

The historical kind: not just a private practice, but an attempt to change the terms for everyone.

---

> Please stop legitimizing LLMs or AI image generators or GitHub Copilot or any of this garbage. I am begging you to stop using them, stop talking about them, stop making new ones, just stop.
> <br><br>
> -- Drew DeVault, [Please stop externalizing your costs directly into my face](https://drewdevault.com/blog/Stop-externalizing-your-costs-on-me/), March 17, 2025

A direct public appeal, on a bill of costs: carbon, freshwater, traumatized labor, scraped work, miserable sysadmins.

---

> What’s hardened are my views on the tech industry, software, management, and influential members of the software developer ecosystem. [...] The more I wrote about generative models, the more appalled I became at the response from the industry, to both my writing and that of others actively highlighting the risks. Few people who have any influence in tech and software seem to care about the harms, the political manipulation, the outright sabotage of education, the association with extremism, or the *literal* child abuse.
> <br><br>
> -- Baldur Bjarnason, [Have I hardened against LLMs?](https://www.baldurbjarnason.com/2026/have-i-hardened-against-ai/), February 9, 2026

Author of *The Intelligence Illusion*, where he describes ChatGPT as "the opposite of good software." For Bjarnason, the downside comprehensively outweighs the upside, and his critique is aimed squarely at an industry and management culture willing to ignore systemic harms, labor exploitation, and software insecurity for the sake of an unproven productivity bump.

---

> Each day we delay the advancement of ML models buys time to learn how to manage technical debt and errors introduced in legal filings. Another day to prepare for ML-generated CSAM, sophisticated fraud, obscure software vulnerabilities, and AI Barbie. Another day for workers to find new jobs.
> <br><br>
> -- Kyle Kingsbury, [The Future of Everything is Lies, I Guess: Where Do We Go From Here?](https://aphyr.com/posts/420-the-future-of-everything-is-lies-i-guess-where-do-we-go-from-here), April 16, 2026

Refuse, organize, regulate - as delay, openly conceded not to be a stop. Same person as the Old Order entry above, different position, which is the point of filing positions instead of people.

---

> The precisely appropriate ways in which to resist AI encroachment on all software development lie well beyond the margins of this one short post. How much you can resist and which specific uses you should resist are up to you. But it is worth resisting in software just as much as it would be worth resisting in any creative medium.
> <br><br>
> -- Glyph, [Programming Isn't Special](https://blog.glyph.im/2026/10/programming-isnt-special.html), October 9, 2026

Draws on John Berger's *Ways of Seeing* to argue that programming - even mundane workday code - is art, and that handing the mundane work to AI removes the practice required to ever make great things.

---

> If we can mitigate the effects that LLMs have on us and reduce the filtering burden, we can, more likely than not, simply outcompete LLM users. After all, LLMs, as we've previously established, are mostly useful to people who are not good at what they do: weak players in our socioeconomic game.
> <br><br>
> -- Iris Meredith, [There's little that's "inevitable" about AI](https://deadsimpletech.com/blog/llms-arent-inevitable), October 10, 2026

Models LLMs not as gunpowder (adopt or be conquered) but as battlefield chemical weapons: useful only to weak players fighting weak players, and neutralizable by regulation, economics, and social opprobrium. Earlier in the year, she spent a week testing coding agents for "[My week with opencode](https://deadsimpletech.com/blog/week-with-opencode)" (January 13, 2026), where she stood at the Mennonite/Old Order boundary - willing at most to "keep a pet local model around to provide input whenever brain-rotted slop is required" and unwilling to release LLM code to the public.

## Romantics

No line left to draw. The diagnosis is accepted, and what remains is grief for the craft as it was - the 1812 hand-loom weaver who has consented to the mill and is mourning the loom.

---

> Writing code by hand gave me the pace of thought I needed to understand a problem deeply.
> <br><br>
> -- Alex Kondov, [Confessions of a Code Monkey](https://thethinkingbuilder.substack.com/p/confessions-of-a-code-monkey), January 23, 2026

---

> Someday years from now we will look back on the era when we were the last generation to code by hand. We'll laugh and explain to our grandkids how silly it was that we typed out JavaScript syntax with our fingers. But secretly we'll miss it.
> <br><br>
> -- Nolan Lawson, [We mourn our craft](https://nolanlawson.com/2026/02/07/we-mourn-our-craft/), February 7, 2026

---

> I wrote millions of lines of code, from scratch; a good chunk of that was without benefit of the Internet, and its infinite reference library. None of it was AI-assisted.
> <br><br>
> -- Peter Rukavina, [What we are losing](https://ruk.ca/content/what-we-are-losing), February 9, 2026

His response to Lawson, from 43 years of professional programming, 1980 to 2023.

---

> The demand for software is not the same as demand for software engineering. The demand for bread today is far higher than in 1800s, yet that did not lead to a corresponding increase in the demand for break-makers.
> <br><br>
> -- Mo Rassam, [Software Engineering is dead and I'm begging you to accept this](https://tharsalys7.substack.com/p/software-engineering-is-dead-and), October 18, 2026

Rassam has migrated: a hand-loom weaver who has gone out into the city to see what factory jobs there are and realized that you can't go home again.

## The English

No line. Full adoption, no stated boundary, enthusiasm - the Amish word for the rest of us.

---

> We've managed to narrow it down to a single principle: You are getting left behind if you do not adopt chat-based programming as your primary modality. There are a few legitimate reasons for not being able to use chop, but they are quickly evaporating as excuses. So call it whatever you like, but to me, as time goes by, the holdouts are just looking stubborn.
> <br><br>
> -- Steve Yegge, [The death of the stubborn developer](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/the-death-of-the-stubborn-developer), December 10, 2024

Nine days after GPT-4 shipped, Yegge had already sounded the horn in [Cheating is all you need](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/cheating-is-all-you-need) (March 23, 2023), declaring LLMs the biggest shift since the World Wide Web. By late 2024, the early warnings in [The death of the junior developer](https://sourcegraph.com/blog/the-death-of-the-junior-developer) hardened into an ultimatum: chat-oriented programming is the primary modality, and anyone resisting is merely stubborn. By mid-2025 there was "nary an IDE in sight" ([The brute squad](https://yegge.ai/essays/the-brute-squad/)), arriving in 2026 at [Welcome to Gas Town](https://yegge.ai/essays/welcome-to-gas-town/): *"It’s also 100% vibe coded. I’ve never seen the code, and I never care to."*

---

> This tale isn't about any particular company, it's about the raging AI bull that's been unleashed which enables anyone, to do anything. [...] The founders didn't intend to slash their workforce; it just happened naturally - people self-selected out of the new AI+tools first direction - which works for now but the places to turn to will soon diminish, fast. [...] Don't fall asleep at the wheel on this one. Invest in yourself - if you’re a high-agency person, there’s never been a better time to be alive...
> <br><br>
> I suspect there's not going to be mass-layoffs for software developers at Companies due to AI, instead there what we will see is a natural attrition between those who invest in themselves right now and those who do not.
> <br><br>
> -- Geoffrey Huntley, [What do I mean by some software devs are "ngmi"?](https://ghuntley.com/ngmi/), February 7, 2025

The sequel to his conversion at the pool in [An "oh fuck" moment in time](https://ghuntley.com/oh-fuck/) (January 14, 2025), where he left Cursor running a Rust-to-Haskell port with CoreAudio FFI while swimming with his kids and returned to find it working, announcing that non-adopters were "frankly not gonna make it." Here he defines the acronym: no mass layoffs required—just a quiet, brutal sorting where developers who dismiss models as hype self-select out while high-agency cyborgs take the wheel.

---

> I've been in the now-renamed Yolo Mode since March 2025. I just let the agents do whatever, to whatever.
> <br><br>
> -- Me, [How I Learned to Stop Coding and Love the Machine](/garden/how-i-learned-to-stop-coding-and-love-the-machine.html)

Whatever this taxonomy says about everyone else, it says that about its author too. I am not immune to propaganda!

## Things That Do Not Fit

The taxonomy above sorts by the extent of acceptable use: who draws the line, and how wide it is. This section logs positions that break those two axes.

### The Butlerian Jihadis

The real-world Amish and Old Order are defined by [*Gelassenheit*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelassenheit) (quiet yieldedness) and [nonresistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonresistance). They keep to themselves, hitch up the buggy, and leave the English alone. Even the historical Luddites were bargaining with mill owners over piecework wages and phased rollouts - violence as a means to an end.

A different posture shares the Old Order's zero-use line, but swaps quiet withdrawal for excommunication, blacklists, and a post-bubble tribunal - or, on the physical fringe that Sean Goedecke documents in "[Blood in the datacenter](https://www.seangoedecke.com/luddites-and-ai-datacenters/)" ("Is it time to start burning down datacenters?"), shots fired at councilmen's houses and firebombs. Filing this posture under Old Order slanders the Amish; filing it under Luddite misses that nobody here is asking for a seat at the bargaining table. The closest name is the one I already borrowed from Frank Herbert, in my [Fomenting the Butlerian Jihad](/garden/fomenting-the-butlerian-jihad.html). *"Thou shalt not make a machine in the likeness of a human mind"* - and anyone who does is a collaborator.

---

> If you personally work on developing LLMs et al, know this: I will never work with you again, and I will remember which side you picked when the bubble bursts.
> <br><br>
> -- Drew DeVault, [Please stop externalizing your costs directly into my face](https://drewdevault.com/blog/Stop-externalizing-your-costs-on-me/), March 17, 2025

---

> We are making this choice. But really, that means you have already decided for me. And I curse you and the ground you walk on for it. No, I'm not joking or exaggerating. Burn in hell. [...] I do not forgive you.
> <br><br>
> -- Larry Garfield, [Selfish AI](https://www.garfieldtech.com/blog/selfish-ai), February 1, 2026

## Taxonomizing Price Shocks

When something gets scarce or expensive, the anger almost always lands sideways - on the other buyer in line. I call this **demand-scolding**.

Sometimes the buyer next to you really is the problem. Usually, the choke point sits upstream. Here is a field guide to shortages and price spikes, sorted by who actually deserves the blame.

| Choke Point | Diagnostic Tell | What Fixes It |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **🏭 Supplier** | Prices jump, margins expand, and unit output stays flat; or wafers and lines are reassigned upstream before a retail SKU is ever made. | Signed long-term volume contracts that take glut risk off the manufacturer, or new entrants breaking concentration. |
| **👮 Regulator** | Prices are capped below clearing levels, causing local dry-outs and hoarding, or new supply sits in a multi-year permitting queue despite buyers paying up front. | Lifting price and allocation controls so arbitrage works; clearing permitting and interconnection queues. |
| **👤 Customer** | Rivals buy the identical finished SKU out of the same retail channel faster than factories can ship, or arbitrageurs hoard stock solely to resell. | Factory volume eventually drowning out inventory hoarding. |

---

## Blame the Supplier

Look here when a handful of firms control production, barriers to entry run into the tens of billions of dollars and multiple years, and a demand surge gets harvested as margin instead of answered with volume.

### 1999-2002 DRAM Price-Fixing Cartel

From April 1999 to June 2002, memory makers conspired to fix the DRAM prices they charged Dell, Compaq, Hewlett-Packard, Apple, IBM, and Gateway.

- **The convictions:** Infineon pleaded guilty in 2004, paid a $160 million fine, and saw four executives sentenced to between four and six months in prison. Hynix, now SK hynix, pleaded guilty in 2005 and paid $185 million. Samsung pleaded guilty in 2005 and paid $300 million, which the Justice Department called the ["second largest criminal antitrust fine in U.S. history,"][doj-2005] and in March 2006 [three Samsung executives][doj-2006] agreed to serve seven or eight months in prison and pay $250,000 apiece. Twelve individuals and four companies were charged, with total fines exceeding $731 million.
- **The informant:** Micron paid nothing. It cooperated under the Justice Department's Corporate Leniency Policy and, by its own account, escaped ["prosecution, fines, or other penalties."][micron-2004] Its CEO, Steve Appleton, acknowledged that "the DOJ's investigation revealed evidence of price fixing by Micron employees and its competitors." One Micron regional sales manager [pleaded guilty to obstruction][doj-2005] and received six months of home detention after withholding and altering subpoenaed grand jury documents.

### 2008-2012 DRAM Glut and Consolidation

Why do memory suppliers hesitate to build ahead of demand? Because the last full capacity race killed the losers and shrank the industry to three main survivors.

- **2008 crash:** After an industry-wide race to add capacity, DRAM prices [fell nearly 75% in 2008][tf-2008], and memory makers lost more than $8 billion across the first three quarters.
- **Qimonda:** In January 2009, Infineon spin-off Qimonda filed for insolvency with 12,000 employees, blaming ["the massive drop in prices in the DRAM industry."][qimonda]
- **Elpida:** In 2012, Elpida [filed for bankruptcy][elpida] with $5.6 billion in debt, the largest bankruptcy by a Japanese manufacturer at the time. Micron bought Elpida out of bankruptcy, and Elpida's fabs [added roughly 45%][micron-elpida] to Micron's manufacturing capacity.

### 2016-2017 DRAM Parallel Cuts

Buyers sued Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron over parallel production cuts in 2016 and 2017. A federal district court dismissed the case, and in March 2022 the Ninth Circuit affirmed, ruling that the cuts were ["more likely explained by lawful, unchoreographed free-market behavior"][dram-ii] in a concentrated industry, even after weighing their "criminal history from twenty years ago."

Under U.S. antitrust law, [conscious parallelism][parallelism] - three companies in a concentrated market looking at the same margin math and independently choosing not to expand - is not itself unlawful, and produces the same supply restriction as a cartel without a phone call.

### 2025-2026 DRAM and HBM Crunch

In the first quarter of 2026, [TrendForce reported][tf-1q] that three firms controlled 89.7% of global DRAM revenue: Samsung at 38.5%, SK hynix at 28.8%, and Micron at 22.4%.

- **Upstream wafer substitution:** AI buyers aren't buying desktop DDR5 sticks at retail. They buy high-bandwidth memory, or HBM - DRAM dies stacked 12 to 16 high - under multi-year contracts directly from the three manufacturers. Each gigabyte of HBM consumes [roughly three times the wafer capacity][toms-hbm] of DDR5. As Micron Chief Business Officer Sumit Sadana told CNBC in January 2026: ["As we increase HBM supply, it leaves less memory left over for the non-HBM portion of the market, because of this three-to-one basis."][cnbc-sadana]
- **Killing the consumer line:** In December 2025, Micron shut down its 29-year-old Crucial consumer memory brand ["in order to improve supply and support for our larger, strategic customers in faster-growing segments."][crucial]
- **Prices doubled, bits didn't:** In Q1 2026, conventional DRAM contract prices rose 93% to 98% quarter-over-quarter and industry revenue jumped 81% to $97 billion, while SK hynix's bit shipments stayed ["broadly in line with the previous quarter"][tf-hynix] as its average selling prices rose about 65%. In Q2 2026, industry revenue climbed another 59.5% to $154.73 billion on modest bit growth, with Q3 consumer DRAM facing the steepest increases ["as suppliers have significantly curtailed supply,"][tf-2q] and Q4 conventional DRAM contract prices forecast to [rise another 10% to 15%][tf-4q].
- **Blaming customers for the 2023 glut:** In June 2026, Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra told CNBC's *Mad Money* that ["certain customers drove pricing significantly down in our industry. In 2023, our prices came down to one-third of what they were,"][cnbc-mehrotra] after Micron had cut its own capital expenditure that year from $12.1 billion to $7.7 billion.
- ***Garciaguirre v. Samsung*:** In June 2026, fourteen individuals and three small PC businesses [sued Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron][toms-suit] in federal court in San Jose. Using TrendForce per-wafer math, [the complaint][complaint] notes that in Q1 2026 a wafer of 64GB DDR5 server modules earned more than a wafer of HBM, arguing that ["leaving that profit unclaimed, in unison, while commodity prices set records, is difficult to reconcile with independent profit maximization."][complaint-p12] The defendants [moved to dismiss][mtd] on September 2, with a hearing set for [November 13, 2026][docket], summarizing their own conduct as: *"three companies in a highly concentrated market independently reduced production amid falling prices during a 'bust' cycle, and then shifted capacity toward more profitable products in response to surging AI-driven demand."*
- **What actually relieves it:** Fabs. Micron is building a new fab in Boise due to ship its first chips in mid-2027, and China's CXMT [plans to expand][tf-cxmt] from roughly 320,000 wafers a month to 420,000 by 2027. When open-hardware maker [PINE64][pine64] paused production in 2026, Hackster's headline blamed AI ["Until the AI Bubble Bursts,"][hackster-pine64] but PINE64's own Mastodon post simply pointed to component pricing ["after mid 2027"][pine64-mastodon] - Boise's delivery window.

### 2026 Nearline Hard Drive Allocation

Early in 2026, Western Digital's CEO stated that the company was ["pretty much sold out for calendar 2026,"][wd] with long-term hyperscaler agreements already locked in for 2027 and 2028, and consumer products accounting for just 5% of revenue.

---

## Blame the Regulator

Look here when prices are forbidden from clearing the market, when supplies are rationed by historical formula rather than current need, or when buyers are ready to finance new capacity that cannot get permission to connect.

### 1971-1981 U.S. Gasoline Price Controls

The [1973 oil crisis][oil-crisis] is remembered for the October 19, 1973 [Arab oil embargo][fed-embargo], a genuine supply-cartel shock that sent crude from $2.90 a barrel to $11.65 by January 1974. Look closer at the domestic gas lines, however, and the distribution breakdown was regulatory.

- **Shortages preceded the embargo:** Nixon [froze wages and prices on August 15, 1971][bradley]. By February 1973 - eight months before the embargo - Senator Henry Jackson was already warning Congress of "an unprecedented breakdown in our energy supply and distribution system."
- **Federal demand-scolding:** On November 25, 1973, Nixon went on television to announce Saturday-night-to-Sunday gas station closures, a 50 mph speed limit, thermostats lowered by six degrees, and dimmed White House Christmas lights, asking Americans for ["the spirit of discipline, self-restraint, and unity."][nixon] Congress fixed the [national speed limit at 55 mph][nmsl] in January 1974, where it stayed until 1995.
- **Allocation by 1972 formula:** Two days after his speech, Nixon signed the [Emergency Petroleum Allocation Act][epaa], which distributed fuel according to what each region had purchased in 1972.
- **Misallocation data:** A 2026 paper by Brian Albrecht, Alex Tabarrok, and Mark Whitmeyer [analyzed the February 1974 station surveys][chaos]: the national gasoline shortfall was about 9%, yet more than 90% of sampled stations in Connecticut and Massachusetts were rationing or dry, while Idaho, Montana, Utah, Hawaii, and Wyoming reported no shortages at all. Because price controls capped what a refiner could earn per gallon everywhere, nothing pulled fuel toward the states that were short: *"Price controls kill the incentive for arbitrage."*
- **Growing towns starved by formula:** In March 1974, the American Automobile Association testified to Congress that Gaithersburg, Maryland received 80% of its 1972 gasoline volume after its population had grown by 50%, urging Congress to ["create a positive program whose purpose is to increase our fuel supply. The present program acts as a disincentive."][jec-1974]
- **Sideways rage at the pump:** Drivers blamed each other. TIME reported in February 1974 that America's 117 million cars had become ["rolling reservoirs of gasoline, making the shortage worse,"][time-fever] as drivers topped off tanks and a Pittsburgh pump attendant spat in a customer's face. States rolled out [odd-even license-plate rationing][time-rationing] with half-tank minimums and fines up to $1,000 in New Jersey and Maryland.
- **How it ended:** On January 28, 1981, Executive Order 12287 exempted crude oil and refined products from price and allocation controls ["effective immediately."][eo-12287]

### 2026-2031 U.S. Grid Interconnection Queue

AI data centers get blamed for rising electricity rates, even though hyperscalers are signing the multi-decade contracts needed to build generation: Microsoft signed a 20-year contract to [restart an 835 MW nuclear reactor at Three Mile Island][crane], and Meta contracted for [433 MW of nuclear uprates][vistra-meta] across three Vistra plants alongside 20 years of output.

The bottleneck is getting generation built and permitted to connect:

- **The permitting queue:** [Berkeley Lab][lbnl-queue] counts roughly 2,061 GW waiting in line for grid interconnection approval: 1,312 GW of generation and 749 GW of storage.
- **The capacity shortfall:** In July 2026, grid operator [PJM][pjm-2028], which serves more than 67 million people across 13 states and Washington, D.C., came up 6,831 MW short of its reliability requirement in its 2028-29 capacity auction; only 525 MW of what cleared came from new plants and uprates.
- **Upstream turbine backlog:** GE Vernova, the largest gas turbine manufacturer, is [booking reservations for 2031][turbines].

---

## Blame the Customer

Look here only when buyers are genuinely fighting over the exact same finished product on the exact same retail shelf - and even then, notice how the fight actually ends.

### 2021 Ethereum GPU Shortage and Nvidia LHR

Unlike HBM vs. DDR5, the 2021 graphics card shortage was a true fight at the retail shelf: crypto miners and gamers wanted the same GeForce RTX 30-series boxes from the same stores on the same launch days.

- **Degrading the product for the "wrong" buyer:** Nvidia tried the remedy demand-scolding implies - [pink margarine](/2026/03/01/pink-margarine.html) in silicon. In February 2021 it shipped the RTX 3060 with driver detection that halved Ethereum hash rates to ["help ensure GeForce GPUs end up in the hands of gamers,"][nvidia-3060] and in May 2021 it extended its "Lite Hash Rate" limiter to the 3060 Ti, 3070, and 3080 for ["more GeForce cards at better prices into the hands of gamers everywhere."][nvidia-lhr]
- **How long it lasted:** Mining software recovered about 70% of the throttled performance within months, and in May 2022 [NiceHash bypassed the limiter completely][toms-nicehash].

### 2020-2023 PlayStation 5 Scalpers

After the PS5 launched in November 2020, scalpers used checkout bots to beat retail buyers to stock and flip consoles at a markup - pure zero-sum rent extraction at the shelf.

- **What killed the scalpers:** Not buyer self-restraint, and not anti-scalping sermons. Sony kept shipping consoles until January 2023, when its gaming chief announced that buyers ["should have a much easier time finding one at retailers globally, starting from this point forward."][verge-ps5] By April 2023, [scalpers were cutting prices below retail][techspot-ps5]. A factory can keep shipping longer than a scalper can stay liquid.

---

## Why Big Buyers Usually Help You Later

Except for pure resale scalpers, massive buyers who bid up a commodity in year one are usually the ones financing the factory that makes it cheap for you in year five.

- **Wright's Law:** In 1936, aeronautical engineer Theodore Wright observed that every doubling of cumulative production cuts unit cost by a steady percentage. Solar panels have followed [Wright's law][owid] for forty years, dropping about 20% in cost per doubling of installed capacity, from $106 a watt to $0.38. Retail hobbyists don't buy enough volume to double cumulative production; hyperscalers do.
- **The 2010s U.S. Shale Boom:** Even when a demand boom is a financial bubble, the physical capacity survives the crash. In the 2010s, U.S. [fracking][fracking] and shale drillers burned through [$300 billion in negative free cash flow, wrote down $450 billion of capital, and filed more than 190 bankruptcies][deloitte] - peaking *"without making money for the industry in aggregate."* The investors lost their money, the wells stayed in the ground, and in 2020 the United States became a [net exporter of petroleum][eia] for the first time since at least 1949.

## Do LLMs Understand "For Each"?

You have a list of items. You need a language model to process each one the same way. Do you write this:

> For each item in the list, perform steps 1 through 5.

Or this:

> **Item 1:** Perform steps 1 through 5.
>
> **Item 2:** Perform steps 1 through 5.
>
> **Item 3:** Perform steps 1 through 5.

The first is compact, elegant, and how a programmer would think about it. The second is verbose, redundant, and feels like it insults the model's intelligence. The research says the second one works better, and the reasons are architectural - rooted in how transformers allocate attention. But whether that architecture actually constrains you depends on how, exactly, you harness the models and what, exactly, you ask them to do.

## The Curse of Instructions

<blockquote class="link-card">
  
  <h1>Curse of Instructions: Large Language Models Cannot Follow Multiple Instructions at Once</h1>
  
  <a href="https://openreview.net/forum?id=R6q67CDBCH" target="_blank" rel="noopener">openreview.net/forum?id=R6q67CDBCH</a>
  
</blockquote>




> The success rate of all the instructions is precisely explained by the success rate of individual instructions to the power of the total number of instructions.

That's the "curse of instructions" (Harada et al., October 2024): individually easy steps compound into near-certain failure at scale. If a model follows any single instruction 95% of the time, 10 simultaneous instructions yield roughly 60% all-correct compliance. In practice, it's worse. GPT-4o managed just 15% success with 10 simultaneous instructions. Claude 3.5 Sonnet did better at 44%, but neither is close to reliable.

When a prompt says "for each of 10 items, follow these 5 steps," the model must satisfy 50 effective constraints in a single generation. The multiplicative decay means that individually easy steps compound into near-certain failure at scale. Unrolling into separate per-item calls keeps each call at 5 constraints, preserving the per-instruction success rate without cross-item compounding.

The [IFScale benchmark][2] (Jaroslawicz et al., July 2025) pushed this further, testing up to 500 simultaneous keyword-inclusion instructions across 20 models from seven providers. Even the best performer - Gemini 2.5 Pro - managed only about 69% accuracy at 500 instructions. More usefully, the study identified three distinct degradation patterns across model families:

- **Threshold decay** for reasoning models like o3 and Gemini-2.5-Pro: near-perfect performance until roughly 150 instructions, then collapse.
- **Linear decay** for models like GPT-4.1 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet: steady, proportional decline.
- **Exponential decay** for smaller or older models like Claude 3.5 Haiku and Llama-4-Scout: steep drops from the start.

This means the penalty for loop-style prompts depends partly on which model you're using. Reasoning models tolerate higher instruction density before degradation kicks in. Smaller models degrade rapidly as instruction count grows.

## Why It Happens

The exponential compounding is a symptom. The disease is architectural.

### Attention Sinks

Researchers at MIT discovered that transformer models dump disproportionate attention onto initial tokens due to [softmax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Softmax_function) normalization - a phenomenon they called "[attention sinks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)" (Xiao et al., September 2023). A [2025 follow-up](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02732) (Barbero et al., April 2025) traced the cause to a fundamental mechanism: LLMs use attention sinks to avoid over-mixing information across layers, and "their formation during training seems inevitable." The original researchers proposed a practical workaround - [StreamingLLM](https://github.com/mit-han-lab/streaming-llm), which adds a dedicated placeholder token to absorb excess attention - but the underlying behavior is architectural.

In a loop-style prompt, the instruction block at the top becomes the attention sink while items in the middle are starved. Unrolling creates fresh attention sinks at each item's instruction header.

### Lost in the Middle

"[Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172)" (Liu et al., July 2023) demonstrated a U-shaped performance curve: models access information at the beginning and end of their context with meaningfully higher accuracy than information in the middle. A follow-up "[Found in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16008)" (Hsieh et al., June 2024) traced this to an intrinsic attention allocation bias that persists regardless of content relevance, and proposed a calibration mechanism to mitigate it. The bias persists in practice - IFScale found systematic favoritism toward earlier instructions across all models tested.[^2] In a loop-style prompt processing many items, the middle items land in the degraded zone. Unrolling gives every item its own beginning and end.

### Causal Masking and Prompt Repetition

The most elegant piece of evidence comes from Google Research. Leviathan, Kalman, and Matias published "[Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs][5]" in December 2025. The finding: simply duplicating the entire prompt improved accuracy on 47 of 70 tested tasks with zero losses. On one task, Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite jumped from 21.33% to 97.33% - a 76 percentage-point gain.

The mechanism is revealing. In causal (left-to-right) attention, instruction tokens are processed before data tokens, meaning the instruction encoding lacks awareness of the data it must operate on. When instructions are repeated *after* the data - or, by extension, repeated per item - each instruction instance can attend to all preceding context, creating a richer signal. Critically, padding the prompt to equivalent length *without* repeating instructions produced no improvement, confirming the gain comes from information repetition, not length.

This has a direct implication for the loop question. Unrolling is not merely about reducing constraint count per call. It's about giving each item its own copy of the instructions, positioned where the instructions can attend to the relevant data. The transformer's causal attention architecture mechanistically favors this.

But there's a wrinkle. The prompt repetition effect was "neutral to slightly positive" for reasoning models (5 wins, 1 loss, 22 neutral out of 28 tasks). Models that reason via chain-of-thought already perform an internal form of "re-reading" that mimics the repetition effect. This aligns with IFScale's finding that reasoning models tolerate higher instruction density.[^2]

## The Cost of Unrolling: Instruction Drift

So far, the case for unrolling looks strong. But unrolling has its own costs.

Repeating instructions N times increases total token count, and as context grows, the relative attention weight of the initial system prompt decreases. Research on [instruction drift][7] (Wen et al., October 2025) formalizes this as "turn-wise divergence from goal-consistent behavior over extended contexts." The drift doesn't accumulate without bound - it stabilizes at finite levels that can be shifted downward by lightweight interventions like goal reminders. But it means that aggressively unrolling a 50-item list into a single massive prompt could erode the very instruction adherence you're trying to preserve.

This creates a tension:

- Loops suffer from exponential constraint compounding.
- Unrolling suffers from linear drift.

For small N, the compounding fix dominates; unroll. For very large N, drift may erode the gains. The crossover point - the sweet spot where you'd make a different design decision - is not precisely characterized in the literature, but the [batch prompting][8] research (Cheng et al., January 2023) suggests a ceiling: batching up to about 4 unrelated items retained quality, with degraded accuracy beyond that.

## The Distinction That Actually Matters

Nearly every study cited so far measures *single-generation* constraint satisfaction. ManyIFEval tests whether 10 formatting constraints are satisfied in one output.[^1] IFScale tests whether 500 keywords appear in one business report.[^2] Chen et al.'s multi-instance processing study (March 2026) tests whether 100 items are processed in one pass.[^9] The attention sink, lost-in-the-middle, and causal masking effects all operate within a single forward pass of the model.

But most people asking "should I unroll my loops?" aren't writing monolithic prompts. They're building [agentic workflows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligent_agent) where the model makes tool calls - reads a file, queries a database, edits a document - and each tool call creates a new generation boundary. In a typical agentic loop:

1. Load guidance rule (tool call, new generation context)
2. Read file (tool call, new generation context)
3. Evaluate (reasoning step)
4. Maybe edit (tool call, new generation context)
5. Back to step 1 for next item

Each tool call resets the generation context. The agent isn't trying to satisfy 15 constraints in one output - it's doing 5 things, getting a response, doing 5 more, getting a response. The exponential compounding from ManyIFEval doesn't apply because each generation carries only a handful of constraints. The positional bias effects are also mitigated, though how much depends on the harness - orchestration frameworks differ in whether and how they re-inject context between tool calls.

The prompt repetition paper implicitly confirms this: its effect is neutral for reasoning models because they already "re-read" internally via chain-of-thought.[^5] Agentic tool-call loops achieve the same re-reading mechanically - each iteration brings the instructions back into focus through the tool response cycle.

The [Multi-Task Inference][6] benchmark (Son et al., February 2024) tests and illustrates this boundary cleanly. When 2-3 closely related subtasks shared a single generation instead of being split apart, GPT-4 improved by up to 12.4%. The authors' explanation: "looking at the next sub-task provides critical clues on the answer format for solving the previous sub-task." 

<div class="polaroid-container">
  <div class="polaroid">
    <a href="arxiv.2402.11597v2.fig1.png">
      <img src="arxiv.2402.11597v2.fig1.png" alt="Multi-Task Inference: Can Large Language Models Follow Multiple Instructions at Once? (Figure 1)" class="polaroid-image">
    </a>
    <div class="polaroid-title">Multi-Task Inference: Can Large Language Models Follow Multiple Instructions at Once? (Figure 1)</div>
    <div class="polaroid-link">
      
      <a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2402.11597v2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">arxiv.org/html/2402.11597v2</a>
      
    </div>
    <small class="polaroid-archive">
      
      (<a href="https://web.archive.org/web/20240607173315/https://arxiv.org/html/2402.11597v2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">archive</a>)
      
    </small>
  </div>
</div>


This is evidence about **where to draw the generation boundary, not evidence for loops.** Once you've partitioned work into per-item units, over-decomposing the steps *within* each item's group can hurt by denying related steps access to one another's context.

This **doesn't mean agentic workflows are immune** to instruction-following failures. The [AGENTIF benchmark][10] (Qi et al., NeurIPS 2025) - the first benchmark specifically designed for instruction following in agentic scenarios - found that current models still struggle, even the best achieving only about 60% constraint satisfaction on agentic prompts averaging nearly 12 constraints each.[^10] Conditional constraints proved particularly fragile: over 30% of failures came from incorrect condition checking - the model failing to recognize whether a condition was triggered, not failing to follow the constraint itself. And meta-constraints - instructions that govern other instructions, like "prioritize X over Y" - were among the least reliable of all.[^10] The constraints-per-generation count still matters. It's just that tool boundaries keep the per-generation count lower than what a monolithic prompt would impose.

There's a deeper prerequisite for successful agentic looping, too. LLMs have effectively zero latent working memory - [Huang et al.][15] (2025) showed that LLMs function as "reactive post-hoc solvers" that reconstruct task state from context at every generation. They don't hold a mental checklist; they re-derive one from the conversation history each turn. As that history grows, reconstruction degrades: open-weight models stop making measurable progress after about 6 steps,[^16] and roughly 23% of multi-agent system failures stem from premature termination, incomplete verification, or looping indefinitely.[^17] For iterative workflows, the fix is to externalize the iteration state - get the "what's done / what remains" tracking out of the model's head and into something it reads back explicitly.

[Anthropic's prompt engineering documentation][11] reflects both of these takeaways. Their guidance explicitly advises externalizing the task list, and notes Claude's reasoning as the reason why you don't have to manually orchestrate multi-step processes anymore:

> Use the first context window to set up a framework (write tests, create setup scripts), then use future context windows to iterate on a todo-list.
> <br>...<br>
> With adaptive thinking and subagent orchestration, Claude handles most multi-step reasoning internally. Explicit prompt chaining (breaking a task into sequential API calls) is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure.

## The Real Question

The most useful insight from integrating this research isn't about loops versus unrolling per se. It's that **the relevant unit of analysis is the generation boundary, not the prompt boundary.**

The research unanimously shows that within a single generation, constraint compounding is exponential and positional bias is real. The practical question is always: **how many constraints am I asking the model to satisfy in this generation?**

If the answer is "few, because tool calls partition the work," loops are fine. If the answer is "many, because this is a monolithic prompt," unroll. The real answer lurking under that decision is that while loops can sometimes work, unrolling - whether in the prompt, the harness, or within the model's reasoning - is basically always being used for handling iterative assignments.

## A Decision Framework

For what it's worth, here's how I'd think about it:

### Single-Generation Prompts

No tool calls, one shot. You're not writing code like this; this is maybe embedded in a production system, part of a data pipeline, or otherwise bundled up and just expected to perform inference once and return a result. Classifiers, judges, etc. In this situation, you're often authoring the harness yourself, and so you get to choose what goes into a "generation" and how to glue results together for the prompt/context of subsequent generations.

These numbers come from different studies at different points in time, conducted against differing sets of models - they're not absolute. Rather, when *you* are having to pick thresholds for your harness' behavior, these numbers may help locate and guide your decision.

| Situation | Approach | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1-3 related items needing cross-reference | Loop with structural markers | Cross-item context sharing may help |
| 4-6 independent items | Partial unrolling with per-item headers; repeat instructions at start and end | The prompt repetition sweet spot |
| 7+ items | Fully unroll into separate API calls | Exponential compounding dominates |
| Any count on smaller/older models | Default to unrolling | Exponential decay from the start |

### Agentic Workflows

Generation boundaries handle the compounding problem. But as noted above, the model still has to track what it's iterating over - and it can't do that reliably from context alone. Externalize the checklist.

| Situation | Approach | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Small set, few steps per item | Loop with tool calls | Generation resets handle compounding; short history keeps state reconstruction reliable |
| Large set or many steps | Externalize the task list; reduce the loop to <ol><li>pull task</li> <li>do task</li> <li>repeat</li></ol> | Models can't reliably track "what's done" in context alone |
| Complex per-item steps (5+ with branching) | Add structural markers within each iteration | Per-generation constraint count still matters |
| 20+ items in one conversation | Periodically re-inject core instructions | Guard against instruction drift[^7] |

Most agent harnesses provide some form of task-list tool for this; writing a checklist to disk can work just as well as [third-party software solutions](https://github.com/gastownhall/beads). The mechanism matters less than the principle: get the "what's done / what remains" state out of the model's head and into something it reads back explicitly.[^Niko]

A personal rule of thumb: I'll start capping any unbroken numbered instruction list at 4 items before a tool call, since the batch prompting research showed meaningful quality degradation beyond that threshold[^8]... *for now!* We might expect this number to creep up as models get better, though it may not be from the underlying Transformer technology but from more-creative and effective behaviors layered on top of it.

### In All Cases

Use structural markers. Whether looped or unrolled, [XML tags](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/use-xml-tags) and markdown headings improve adherence by providing the kind of hierarchical boundaries that models have internalized from their training data. OpenAI's [GPT-4.1 prompting guide](https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide) found that XML performed well for multi-document inputs while JSON performed particularly poorly.

```xml
<task index="1">
## Acme Corp
Evaluate this contract for renewal risk.
</task>

<task index="2">
## Globex Inc
Evaluate this contract for renewal risk.
</task>
```

If you must keep many items in a single prompt, three mitigations improve compliance: 

1. repeat the core instruction block after each item or at the end of the prompt[^5],
2. use indexed structural tags for each item[^12],
3. add a self-verification step asking the model to check whether it completed all items[^13]

## Think in Generations

The transformer's causal attention architecture mechanistically favors explicit, per-item instruction blocks over abstract loop constructs. This is not a prompting trick - it's a consequence of how softmax attention, causal masking, and positional encoding interact. The research evidence for this is strong, converging from multiple independent programs.

But "always unroll" is an oversimplification that fails to account for how most people actually use language models today. In agentic workflows, tool-call boundaries act as natural generation resets that mitigate the very problems unrolling solves. The real skill is learning to think in terms of constraints-per-generation rather than constraints-per-prompt.

The research also suggests this isn't something models will simply "grow out of." [Recent work on compositional generalization][14] (Chang et al., May 2025) argues that for tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning - the logical equivalent of a loop - the training data requirement grows quadratically with token set size.[^14] The limitation is architectural, not parametric. Scaling model size doesn't linearly improve loop handling.

So: unrolling works, the reasons it works are well-understood, and the situations where it doesn't matter are equally well-defined. The question was never really "loop or unroll?" It was "how many things am I asking the model to hold in its head at once?" That question has a precise, architecturally grounded answer. It's just not always the same one.
